definitions.meaning: first meaning: a police officer, who nicks (arrests) people
second meaning: the reddish-brown metallic element

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nicks' suggests a thief stealing metal; in British slang to nick is also to arrest, and a copper is a policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is everyday British slang for a police officer and also the name of the chemical element Cu.

parts.note: a keep is the strongest tower of a castle, so stands for the castle
informally, a hairy situation is a risky one

explanation.surface: Hang on to a shaggy book.
explanation.walkthrough: Castle Dangerous is the last novel by Walter Scott, published in 1831.
explanation.definitionFit: Castle Dangerous is a historical novel by Sir Walter Scott, his final completed work.

clue.text: Schemes involving one servant, a person on the level?

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: schemes are plans
the Roman numeral for one
a manservant

explanation.surface: A plot with a servant in it, and a question about who is honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the level' usually means honest, but here it means living on flat land, the plains.
explanation.definitionFit: A plainsman lives on the plains, flat open country, so is literally a person on level ground.

parts.note: an end is an aim or purpose
the ear is the organ that listens

explanation.surface: Charm someone who listens attentively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intent' looks like an adjective, focused, but it is the noun meaning purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear yourself is to win someone's affection, to win them over.

parts.note: a dentist caps a tooth by crowning it; caps and crowns are the same thing
the Roman numeral for one
Latin for with, as in 'house cum office'

explanation.surface: A cryptic question about crowning someone with a vegetable, like a harvest king.
explanation.definitionFit: Capsicum is the botanical name for the sweet pepper, a common vegetable.

clue.text: Love affair starts to annoy most of us

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the two words
belonging to us

explanation.surface: An affair that begins to irritate nearly everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of us' looks like a phrase meaning the majority; it splits into the end of the first piece and a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Amour is the French loan-word for a love affair, especially a secret one.

clue.text: Detective story by Haggard — left in lurch?

parts.note: She is the adventure novel by H. Rider Haggard

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: to rock is to sway or lurch
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A detective story by Haggard, asking whether someone was abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left in the lurch' means abandoned, but here 'left' is a single letter placed inside a word for lurch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes is the famous fictional detective, so his first name stands for any sleuth.

parts.note: the abbreviation found on taps
an arm or leg is a member of the body

explanation.surface: A chilly club member goes up a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a club member, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A climb is an act of going up, so the noun is a synonym of ascent.

wordplay.note: coins are cash, and three of them puts the word for cash down three times in a row

explanation.surface: A reference to the 1954 film song 'Three Coins in the Fountain'.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis tempts you to complete 'Three Coins in the Fountain'; instead take 'coins' as cash and write it three times. The answer is a 1976 ABBA hit.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a 1976 single by the Swedish pop group ABBA, whose title repeats one word for cash three times.

indicators.note: something broken has been smashed and its pieces reassembled differently

parts.note: the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Someone indicates a cracked spittoon.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuspidor is the American word for a receptacle to spit into.

clue.text: And on came stupid comic, joke teller

indicators.note: comic means funny or ridiculous, so the preceding words are put into a silly new order

parts.note: the four words supply all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A dim-witted comedian walked on stage and told jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' reads as a noun for the performer, but it is the adjective that signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-up comedian performs alone on stage, telling a string of jokes to the audience.

clue.text: House in city on the Lune

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a royal dynasty of medieval England
second meaning: the Lancashire city standing on the River Lune

explanation.walkthrough: 'House' suggests a building, but here it is a royal family line; the Lune is a river in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Lancaster was the dynasty of Henry IV to VI, and Lancaster is the city on the River Lune.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to urge or petition a politician
second meaning: a foyer just inside the door

explanation.surface: Reporters gathered in a building's foyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the newspaper reporters, but it is the verb meaning to put pressure on legislators.
explanation.definitionFit: To lobby is to campaign to influence lawmakers, and a lobby is also a reception area or vestibule.

indicators.note: merry here means tipsy, and a tipsy word staggers into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A pantomime performer put on a cheerful show.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantomime is the British Christmas family theatre show, in which the dame is a comic older woman played by a man.
explanation.definitionFit: The dame is the stock comic female role in British pantomime, traditionally played by a male actor.

clue.text: Gambling game attended by Italian chap in Riviera resort

parts.note: monte is a card game, as in three-card monte
a common Italian man's name

explanation.surface: An Italian man plays cards for money at a seaside resort on the Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: Monte Carlo is the district of Monaco on the French Riviera, famous for its casino.

clue.text: They must accommodate girl over in Greek region

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to take them in, so one word holds the other

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: People in Greece must give a girl a place to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Thessaly is a region of central Greece, a broad plain east of the Pindus mountains.

parts.note: plump and round both mean chubby
a worm is a contemptible person

explanation.surface: A fat, nasty sponger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parasite' suggests a scrounging person, but it is the literal intestinal creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundworms are nematodes, many of which live as parasites inside animals.

parts.note: a trap is a light horse-drawn carriage

indicators.note: rarely here means in an unusual way, so the letters take an uncommon order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A monk riding in a carriage seldom gives gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rarely' reads as 'seldom', but here it signals the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trappist is a monk of the strict Cistercian order of La Trappe, known for silence.

parts.note: surface reading: someone who cannot cope with pressure or criticism
setter's reading: 'it' is alcohol, and the person cannot or will not drink it

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'can't take it' usually means unable to endure hardship; here 'take' means consume and 'it' means drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A teetotaller abstains from alcohol, so is someone who does not take a drink.

parts.note: still and but both mean nevertheless
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An island that remains English.
explanation.walkthrough: Bute is an island in the Firth of Clyde, in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Bute is a Scottish island in the Firth of Clyde, west of Glasgow.

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
veal is calf meat

explanation.surface: Talk about meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal is to disclose or make known, so it shares the sense of telling a secret.

clue.text: Provide witty remark after end of charade

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
a quip is a witty remark

explanation.surface: Someone makes a clever comment once a game of charades is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the remark behind the letter, so the letter comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To equip someone is to furnish or supply them with what they need.

indicators.note: something removed is taken away, so those letters drop out

parts.note: soiled means dirty
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A pawnbroker has had a dirty item taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is old British slang for a pawnbroker; 'article' suggests a pawned item but is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: In old British slang a pawnbroker was called 'uncle', as in 'my watch is at my uncle's'.

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out in a muddled order

parts.note: the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Something very smart has been made into a capital, or excellent, thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as the old exclamation meaning splendid, but it is the definition: a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Amsterdam is the constitutional capital city of the Netherlands.

parts.note: taken as written
a base is a foundation

explanation.surface: Undermine a foundation's dignity.
explanation.definitionFit: To abase someone is to lower them in dignity or esteem, to humble them.

clue.text: One Columbian, one drunk on very rare occasions

indicators.note: a drunk person's words come out jumbled, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: the three words supply all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A man from Colombia, and another person, are only seldom drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something that happens hardly ever, like a second full moon in one month.

clue.text: Climbing plant cute ape chewed up

parts.note: sweet and cute both mean endearing

indicators.note: something chewed up is mangled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sweet little monkey chews up a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a fragrant garden flower that climbs by tendrils up supports.

parts.note: the initial letter shown, before the dashes
limey is American slang for a British person

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at a bleeped-out insult aimed at a British person.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes look like a censored swear word, but they show the answer is B followed by a five-letter word for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Blimey is a British exclamation of surprise, just like 'my word!'
